newsitem.title: UK: Race for UK Conservative leader too close to call.
newsitem.headline: Race for UK Conservative leader too close to call.

text.p: The battle for the leadership of Britain's defeated Conservative Party took a bizarre turn in the runup to the final ballot on Thursday when its leading right winger formed an alliance with his former arch foe.

Kenneth Clarke, the left-leaning former finance minister who has fought to keep Britain's options open on joining a single currency, tipped the scales in his favour when his ideological opposite, John Redwood, joined his side.
The announcement of the unity ticket set the stage for a dramatic down-to-the-wire vote when the 164 Conservative members of parliament will choose their next leader.
The odd-couple pairing, designed to prevent former Welsh secretary William Hague of the party's middle right from winning, shocked many Conservatives and infuriated others.
Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher left no doubt about what she thought of the deal.
"I am supporting William Hague. Now have you got the name," she joked with reporters.
"I come out firmly for William because the principles that he is founding his vision upon are very much the principles I founded my government on for quite a long time."
Although she does not have a vote, Thatcher still wields considerable influence within the party and could influence the outcome.
Hague, who at 36 would be one of the youngest Conservative leaders if he wins, chided the deal struck by Redwood in exchange for the job of opposition finance spokesman if Clarke succeeds.

"In the whole of this campaign I have not offered a job to a single member of parliament. The new leader of the Conservative Party needs freedom of action and to be beholding to no one," he told a news conference.
Clarke, with 64 votes, edged past Hague with 62 in the second ballot on Tuesday. Redwood was forced to drop out after coming in third with 38. It is his supporters who will decide Thursday's outcome.
Clarke and Redwood portrayed their deal as an attempt to end the divisions over Europe that contributed to the Conservative party's overwhelming defeat in the May 1 election.
"In the leadership election campaign I made it very clear we needed to bring an end to the civil war in the Conservative Party," said Redwood.
"I decided the right thing to do was to see if we could mend the party another way by the construction of an honourable peace."
But Peter Tapsell, a Hague supporter, saw it differently.

"His so-called deal with Ken Clarke is quite unacceptable. It's unprincipled, an alliance between opposites. It's just a cheap political deal really, and rather discreditable," he told BBC television.
Political experts said late on Wednesday the race was too close to call and lobbying for the crucial votes would continue into the night. The result will be announced after 1600 GMT on Thursday.
